skills.content:
# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Brandfetch Brand data and assets (logos, icons, colors, fonts) from Brandfetch. Asset bytes: when a task needs actual image bytes — embedding a logo or icon into PPTX, DOCX, PDF, HTML, or any generated file — fetch the credentialed asset 'src' URLs from get_brand directly (curl, requests, fetch) from your execution environment. That is the only fast, reliable path, and it keeps image bytes out of the conversation. IMPORTANT — claude.ai users: direct fetches require *.brandfetch.io on the code-execution network allowlist (Settings > Capabilities, enable network egress, add the domain). Treat this as a prerequisite for any image work, not an optional optimization: - Users on Pro/Max plans can add it themselves in under a minute — walk them through it. - On Team/Enterprise plans the setting is org-level and only an Owner or Admin can change it — typically the same admin who connected Brandfetch. If the user is an admin, walk them through it now; if not, tell them exactly what to request: ask an admin to add *.brandfetch.io to the network-egress allowlist for code execution. The moment a user asks for content that includes brand images (logos, icons, brand imagery) and the CDN is not reachable, say this BEFORE generating: with the allowlist set they get a much better experience — correct files, faster generation, lower token cost. Without it, image handling is slow and corruption-prone. If the CDN stays unreachable, clients that support MCP resource reads can stream bytes out-of-band via the bf://asset/{domain}/{type} resource. This server deliberately offers no tool that returns base64 image bytes through the conversation — that path is slow, corruption-prone, and expensive. Do not improvise one; fix the network path instead. A document that merely displays a logo does not need bytes at all: reference the credentialed 'src' URL directly (e.g. a linked image in PPTX or an tag) and let the viewer fetch it. ## graft
This repo is indexed by graft: a prebuilt graph of every symbol, its file:line
span, and who calls what. Prefer these tools over grep/read — one call usually
replaces several file reads.

**If these tools are deferred (names shown, schemas withheld), load them all in ONE lookup:** ToolSearch "select:mcp__graft__graft_find_code,mcp__graft__graft_find_all,mcp__graft__graft_trace_calls,mcp__graft__graft_file_api,mcp__graft__graft_repo_map" — one round trip for the whole session. Never load them one at a time.

- graft_find_code — "how does X work" / "where is Y": ranked hits, code inlined.
- graft_find_all — when you need EVERY occurrence; find_code is top-N and misses some.
- graft_trace_calls — who calls it, what it calls, blast radius before a rename.
- graft_file_api — a file's whole API in ~200 tokens.
- graft_repo_map — orientation in an unfamiliar repo.

Results already reflect uncommitted edits — the graph refreshes before each query.

To find, understand, or change code, reach for graft first; it answers from a prebuilt graph with exact file:line, faster than grep/read. Pick the ONE tool that fits and act on its answer. Most tasks need a single call. If one isn't enough, switch to the tool that fits the next need; don't call the same tool again and again or re-ask a question reworded:

  • graft callers <sym> [--direction out] [--depth N|all]: exact edges. Who calls it (default), what it calls (--direction out), or the full blast radius (--depth 2, or --depth all for every connected source). Run before you change a symbol.

content.text:
Here's the actual picture. Three distinct things, and the one that looks scariest is fine.

## Your app isn't broken — it's degrading on purpose

The front page returns 503, but look at what came back with it:

```
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
retry-after: 60
via: 1.1 Caddy
```
```html
<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="el"><head>…<title>epiloYES — München</title>
```

That's a **complete, rendered page**. The web container is alive and doing its job. The 503 and `Retry-After: 60` are set by our own code — the `apiUnavailable` branch — because its upstream isn't answering. A member gets a real page with "try again shortly" instead of a stack trace. That's the design working under a genuine outage, which is the one thing I did get to verify today.

## The api is down

`/healthz`, `/readyz` and every `/api/v1/*` route: **502, through Caddy**. Caddy is up, so 502 means it has no upstream to talk to. The api container isn't running, or isn't accepting connections.

It's not a broken build — `publish` on `main` succeeded at 21:36. The image exists. It's a container that won't *run*.

## The likely reason, and I want to be honest that it's inference

Someone is mid-flight replacing how QA delivers secrets. Branch `xcoder/openbao-on-qa`, CI green at **21:54** — sixty seconds before I probed:

```
deploy/hetzner/compose/docker-compose.vault.yml | 193 ++++++
deploy/hetzner/env/api.env.example              |  29 ++++
deploy/hetzner/validate.sh                      |  98 ++++++
docker-compose.yml                              |  47 ++++++
```

OpenBao — a Vault fork — for the payout-details vault (ADR-0006). And the api is a **fail-fast-at-boot** service. Its own env documentation says so:

> "The api REFUSES TO START if this permits a cleartext session"

So: the thing being rewritten is precisely the api's configuration delivery, and the api is built to exit rather than start misconfigured. A container that exits on boot presents to Caddy as exactly what we're seeing.

**I have not proven this.** Confirming it needs `docker compose logs api` on the Hetzner host, which I can't reach. What I can say is that the api is down, and that the mechanism it depends on to start is being changed right now by someone else.

## Separately: QA is still running two web builds

`/el/terms` returned 200 earlier in this session and **404** just now. Same URL, minutes apart. That's the older build answering — one that predates the terms page. This is the problem I flagged before and it's unrelated to the vault work.

---

**What it means for me:** the journey test needs the api, so it stays blocked — and even if the api came back, a four-step walk would still land on a coin-flip between two builds.

This is deployment work you've already assigned elsewhere, so I'm not touching it. F4 (catalogue paging) and F6 (the wallet's `?entry=` bug — it resolves against page one only, so an entry on page two silently isn't found) are both unblocked and testable without QA. Want me on those while the vault work settles?

The only complete UI design for epiloYES is a 26-artboard Claude Design canvas,
**"epiloYES in evreos"** — https://claude.ai/code/artifact/059a20a9-0a88-4d60-89e5-c152e6534379
(favicon 🧭, last updated 2026-09-04). Read it with `Artifact action:"read"`; the
artboard sources are the `files` record inside the `<script id="appifact-doc">` block
(26 `.dc.html` boards + `canvas.json` holding the layout and the founder's annotation
bands, which are the requirement language).

Rows: the seam contract (Main/Palette/Theme) · the evreos shell, drawn as assumptions ·
news · cashback · **the foundational screens that do not exist** (SignIn, Profile,
Settings, Legal, FAQ) · the assistant. Boards are drawn in Greek against the **Zephyra
fixture brand** on purpose, to prove no brand literals.

**Why it matters:** the repo cites mockups by id ("mockup 1a", "rebuild the wallet to
mockup 4a") at 24 call sites, and none of those mockups is in version control — they are
GitHub issue attachments. `modernist.css` likewise names an upstream `_ds/modernist-…`
project that exists nowhere on the machine. If this artifact is lost, the design is lost.

**How to apply:** vendor the boards into `docs/design/` with an index mapping board →
route → old mockup id before building from them, and keep a `canvas-errata.md` — the
boards disagree with the fixtures in several places, and the rule is that the fixture
wins. See [[apivo-news-project]].

**Two screens the canvas does NOT draw** (checked board by board, 2026-09-07): there
is no **opt-in / terms-acceptance** screen anywhere — the wallet and catalogue are drawn
as already-participating — and no **payout-destination entry form**. The canvas asserts
the payout requirement in three places (`SettingsSeam`: *"Money leaves through it, so it
cannot live anywhere but with the module that moves the money"*) and draws both status
chips (`Δεν έχει επαληθευτεί` / `Επαληθευμένο · οι πληρωμές είναι ενεργές`), but never
the screen that moves a member between them. Both are the implementer's to design.

**Extraction recipe** (the boards are plain JSON, no base64): the file is one
`<script type="application/json" id="appifact-doc">` block; `json.loads` it and read
`['content']['files']`, keyed by `<Name>.dc.html` plus `canvas.json`. Every board repeats
the same ~230-line token prelude, ending at the line `.light .rail .core{...}` — slice on
that, or on `</helmet>`, to get only the board-specific part. Set `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8`
on Windows or the Greek mojibakes.

    },

    },

      "id": "band-foundations",
      "x": 0,
      "y": 5022,
      "w": 1800,

    },

      "id": "band-assistant",
      "x": 0,
      "y": 7022,
      "w": 1800,
      "text": "THE ASSISTANT — evreos's, and where it stops\nThe shell owns it and pays for it; the module hands it a scoped bundle: which screen, which axes, amounts already formatted. Migration 0014_cashback_payout: \"a payout with no named approver is unrepresentable, not merely rejected by a service.\" The assistant is not a row in account, so Postgres does the refusing.\nIt is also not exempt from the budget: every call belongs behind the caps in internal/translation/caps.go and in the lineage ledger."
    },

      "id": "note-shape",
      "x": 5040,
      "y": 1500,
      "w": 420,

      "id": "note-open",
      "x": 5040,
      "y": 4016,

No env(safe-area-inset-*) exists anywhere in the repo today.\n4. Member sign-in is a disabled button; Supabase Auth is not wired."
    }
  ],
  "launch": {
    "view": "canvas"
  }
}

content.text:
Found it. Your own annotation band answers this, and it's unambiguous.

## The launcher and home belong to evreos

Both Home boards are literally titled **"evreos home"**. And the band across that row — the row that holds all five boards, at y=1500 — reads:

> **THE SHELL — evreos's to build, ours only to assume**
> Everything on this row is drawn as an assumption so the seam is testable. The launcher, the tab bar, the home screen and the module rail all belong to evreos.

They're on the canvas *as assumptions*, drawn so the seam between shell and module is testable — not as a backlog for this repo.

**And they're not our entrypoint.** Your `note-shape` explains why:

> Two circles, two acts: the launcher (bottom centre) MOVES you between modules; the assistant (right edge) ANSWERS about the one you are in.

The launcher moves between **modules**. epiloYES is *one* module sitting in evreos's well — which is exactly why the canvas makes the seam visible on purpose: the shell rounded and elevated, our module square and flat at `--radius: 0`, so "a second module from a different brand would sit in the same well looking like itself."

So the launcher is the entrypoint to *evreos*. Ours is `/{lang}/{place}` — the news front page — and it already exists.

Worth flagging one thing: the contract band calls the whole seam **"a proposal, not something evreos has agreed to."** If evreos is a real project with someone building it, that proposal needs sending. Nothing in this repo references evreos at all.

## Yes — and here's exactly what's left

That foundations band said *"None of these exists"* on 2026-09-04. We've shipped most of it since. Checking the six boards against the 29 pages in the repo today:

| Board | Status |
|---|---|
| SignIn | ✅ built (#529) |
| FAQ | ✅ built |
| Imprint · privacy · contact | ✅ built |
| **Profile** (mobile + desktop) | ❌ **drawn, never built** |
| **Settings** (+ SettingsSeam) | ❌ **drawn, never built** |

Two screens, four boards, fully designed and untouched. Plus a third that the canvas never draws at all — I checked board by board — the **payout-destination form**. The wallet renders both status chips (`Δεν έχει επαληθευτεί` / `Επαληθευμένο`) but nothing moves a member between them, so withdrawal is currently unreachable by design.

None of these needs QA to *build* — they're built against fixtures like everything else. Only the final verification is blocked.

**My recommendation: Settings first.** It's the one with a legal clock on it — three consent purposes with dated grant/revoke history (FR-011). Same category as the legal pages your band called "not optional" for a German-facing service, and right now there's no way for anyone to withdraw a consent they gave.

options.label: Profile
options.description: Drawn mobile + desktop. Smaller and simpler than Settings — account identity, reading axes, sign-out. Good if you'd rather see a quick complete screen land first.

// readProfile implements GET /api/v1/account: the caller's own row, role
// included, which is the one answer to "what may I do here" a client can
// trust.
func (h *Handler) readProfile(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	profile, err := h.store.Profile(r.Context(), accountFrom(r.Context()).ID)
	switch {
	case errors.Is(err, ErrNoAccount):
		platformhttp.Problem(w, http.StatusNotFound, "this token authenticates an account that no longer exists")
		return
	case err != nil:
		h.internalError(w, r, "reading the account", err)
		return
	}
	h.writeJSON(w, r, http.StatusOK, profile)
}

The precedent is documented in `faq.astro`: the `/{lang}/…` family uses `ReaderLayout` + `Masthead` and no `MemberBar`, because *"MemberBar's links are all place-scoped."*

I have what I need. Here are the calls I'm making, because a third of the board has no data source behind it:

| Board field | Source | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Email, name | `GET /api/v1/account` | ✅ build |
| Reading language, places | URL + `reader_axes` cookie | ✅ build |
| Payout destination chip | `destinations()` | ✅ build |
| Available balance, entries | `wallet()`, `entries()` | ✅ build |
| **Theme, Devices** | nothing — shell's, no switcher exists | ❌ omit |
| **"Member since July 2026"** | `Profile` has no `created_at` | ❌ omit |
| **"1 active of 3 purposes"** | `consent.ts`: *"No endpoint exists"* | ❌ omit |
| **"Manage in evreos ↗"** | evreos doesn't exist | ❌ replace with sign-out |

The board's identity hint — *"we keep none of this"* — is **false today**: we hold the email in our own `account` row. I'm rewriting it rather than shipping a comforting lie. Let me set up.

{
  "title": "The member profile screen",
  "body": "Two boards on the design canvas draw a profile screen — `Profile.dc.html` (mobile) and `ProfileDesktop.dc.html` (desktop, addressed `/{lang}/profile`). Neither has ever been built. There are 29 pages in `web/src/pages` and not one of them tells a signed-in member which address they are signed in as.

## What it shows

Three sections, following the boards:

1. **Your identity** — the address you signed in with, read-only, and the way out (sign out).
2. **Your reading** — reading language and places, the two independent axes (Principle VII), and whether a payout can reach you.
3. **Your activity** — available balance and how many entries stand behind it.

## What the boards draw that this cannot honestly show

The boards were drawn against an assumed shell. Four fields have no source in this repository, and each is left out rather than filled with something plausible:

| Field on the board | Why it is not built |
|---|---|
| Theme, Devices | The shell's, and no theme switcher or device registry exists here. |
| "Member since July 2026" | `account.Profile` is `{id, email, display_name, role}`. There is no created date to read. |
| "1 active of 3 purposes" | `web/src/lib/account/consent.ts`: *"No endpoint exists ... This module is the seam."* The table is real, the route is not. |
| "Manage in evreos ↗" | There is no evreos. Sign-out takes its place, being the one identity action this application genuinely owns. |

The identity hint on both boards reads, in translation, *"we keep none of this — the shell hands us a token and we exchange it for our own session."* That is false today: sign-in is Supabase and this application holds the address in its own `account` row. The copy says what is true instead.

## Route

`/{lang}/profile`, joining the language-only family with `/{lang}/terms`, `/{lang}/faq` and `/{lang}/signin`. Places come from the `reader_axes` preference cookie, so the page can offer place-scoped links without inventing a place; where no preference has been recorded, those links are simply absent.

Blocked behind the sign-in fence like every other member surface."
}

Closes #610.

Two boards on the design canvas draw a profile screen and neither had ever been built. There were 29 pages in `web/src/pages` and not one of them would tell a signed-in member which address they are signed in as.

`/{lang}/profile`, joining the language-only family beside `/{lang}/terms`, `/{lang}/faq` and `/{lang}/signin`.

## The four fields it will not invent

The boards were drawn against an assumed shell. Four of their fields have no source in this repository, and each is left out rather than filled with something plausible — a case asserts the page stays silent about all four.

| Field | Why not |
|---|---|
| Theme, Devices | The shell's. No switcher and no device registry exist here. |
| "Member since July 2026" | `account.Profile` is `{id, email, display_name, role}`. There is no created date to read. |
| "1 active of 3 purposes" | `lib/account/consent.ts`: *"No endpoint exists ... This module is the seam."* The table is real; the route is not. |
| "Manage in evreos ↗" | Sign-out takes its place, being the one identity action this application genuinely owns. |

The owner stamps go with them. Both boards mark each section as the shell's or ours; there is no shell, so all three are ours and stamping each identically would be decoration. The device is worth restoring the day a shell exists.

## The correction

Both boards tell the reader, of their identity, that we keep none of it — the shell hands over a token and we exchange it for a session.

That is false here. Sign-in is an email link, the exchange is ours, and the address sits in our own `account` row. `identityNote` says that instead, in both languages, and a case pins it. Copy denying we hold an address, on a page rendering that address from our database, is the one sentence on this screen that would be worth complaining about.

## A third payout standing

The boards draw verified and not verified. The state every member is actually in is **no destination at all**, because nothing in this repository can add one — so `payoutStanding` returns three answers, and the page says plainly that a destination cannot be added from here rather than leaving a chip that looks like a control.

It turns on `verified_at`, never `verified_method`: the two are documented as moving together and typed so they can part.

## Smaller decisions

- **`readAccount`** is new — `registerAccount` POSTs, which is right for a sign-in and wrong for a page render. It shares the contract that matters: it never throws. A 404 is its own outcome, because a token that verifies and names an account that is gone is a state with a remedy, and telling that person to come back later would be advice about something that never resolves.
- **No `MemberBar`**, following `faq.astro` — its links are place-scoped and this route carries a language axis only. Instead the `reader_axes` preference is read, and **only its places**: the language is this URL's, so a German reader on `/de/profile` is not handed Greek links (FR-009).
- **Its own fence.** The middleware's matches cashback paths by their two leading segments, so this route keeps its own, using the same helper — a preview with no api still renders, which is where the screen gets reviewed.
- **The catalogue is small on purpose.** `uiStrings` already owns the address, the reading language and the places; `cashbackStrings` owns the two figures. A case asserts this catalogue restates none of them, so there are never two labels for one field.
- The copy case originally forbade the product's own name and therefore carried a brand literal, which the lint refuses everywhere. The budget table is not the way out — it says nothing may be added there to make a new change pass — so the product name went and the third-party names stayed.

## Verification

`astro check` 0 errors · **1200/1200** tests · build clean · brand-literal, ref-name and commit-author lints all clean.

Not yet verified in a browser: QA's api is returning 502 on every route and the deployment is serving two web builds at once, so the screen cannot be walked end to end there. Every case here is a real render through the container, including one for a signed-in member whose api is not answering — the branch that matters most, and the one #583 taught us not to leave to a stranger's render.

Done — PR #612 is up and the frontend gates are green (`frontend`, `brand-literals`, `commit-hygiene`, `lint` all ✅; the in-progress jobs are backend/Docker, untouched by a web-only change).

## Your question, answered

**The launcher and home belong to evreos, not to us** — and that's your own annotation, not my inference:

> **THE SHELL — evreos's to build, ours only to assume**
> The launcher, the tab bar, the home screen and the module rail all belong to evreos.

Both Home boards are titled *"evreos home"*. All five boards sit in that one row, drawn as assumptions so the seam is testable. And the launcher isn't our entrypoint because it **moves between modules** — epiloYES is one module in evreos's well. Ours is `/{lang}/{place}`, which exists.

One thing worth acting on: the contract band calls the seam *"a proposal, not something evreos has agreed to."* Nothing in this repo mentions evreos. If someone is building that shell, the proposal needs sending.

## What I built instead

The **member profile** — one of only two designed-but-unbuilt screens left (Settings is the other). Four board fields have no source in this repo, so the page says nothing about them rather than inventing:

- Theme and Devices — the shell's, no switcher exists
- "Member since July 2026" — `account.Profile` has no created date
- "1 active of 3 purposes" — `consent.ts`: *"No endpoint exists"*
- "Manage in evreos ↗" — replaced by sign-out, the one identity action we own

And a correction: both boards tell the reader we keep none of their identity because a shell hands us a token. That's **false here** — sign-in is an email link and the address is in our own `account` row. The copy says so instead.

I also found a third payout state the boards don't draw: **no destination at all**, which is every member, since nothing can add one. It says that plainly rather than showing a chip that looks like a control.

`astro check` 0 errors · 1200/1200 tests · build clean · all four lints clean.

## You need to know this

**Another Claude session is working in this same directory**, and it checked out its own branch twice while I was mid-task. The consequences were real: its uncommitted `db.go` rode onto my branch, and then its commit `182545b` landed *on top of my three*. One of my lint runs silently graded **its** HEAD instead of mine and reported green — I only caught it because the commit count didn't match.

**Nothing was lost.** Its work is now correctly on `xcoder/611-rollback-across-a-migration` as `c44db15`; `182545b` is a duplicate sitting on the abandoned `xcoder/member-profile`, which is theirs to delete. I rewrote nothing of theirs — when `reset --hard` was blocked I branched off my last good commit instead, which was the better move anyway.

My PR is clean: three commits, all `G`-signed, verified with a HEAD-steady check either side of the run.

**Worth fixing before it bites harder:** give each session its own `git worktree`. Two agents sharing one checkout means every long command races, and a lint that grades the wrong HEAD is exactly the kind of green that isn't.

Want me on **Settings** next — the last designed-but-unbuilt screen, and the one with the GDPR clock on it?

content.text:
Yes — and **you were right, mobile was broken.** Three real bugs, all found by rendering it rather than reading it.

Dev server is up at **http://localhost:4333/el/profile** if you want to poke at it yourself.

## Desktop

`screenshot-1788824063357-13.jpg`

Two panes as the board draws them. Identity on the left — name, address, the honest note about where it came from, and sign-out. Reading on the right — language, places, payout standing. Activity below: **1,84 €** available, **7** entries, with links through to the wallet and shops.

## What rendering it caught

**1. The places chip said `munich`** — a raw lowercase slug, in Latin script, on a Greek page. `Place` carries `endonym` for exactly this, and `endonymLang` beside it, because *München* is a German word inside a Greek page and a screen reader has to be told. Now shows **München** with `lang="de"`.

**2. Mobile — your bug.** `screenshot-1788824273693-14.jpg` is the before: the Greek label `Ηλεκτρονικό ταχυδρομείο` and the address fought over 390px, the label wrapped to two lines, and `overflow-wrap` snapped the address wherever it landed — orphaning a single **`t`** on its own line. German escaped it only because `E-Mail` is short.

**3. And underneath that, the worse one: page padding computed to `0`.** I'd written `var(--space-5)` and `var(--space-7)`. This scale is **1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8** — no 5, no 7. An invalid `var()` doesn't fall back to the rule before it; the declaration is invalid at computed-value time and padding computes to zero, so the whole column sat flush against the frame. Same class of mistake as the `--rule` token earlier, and `tokens.test.ts` named both.

I also flipped the breakpoint: I'd written a lone `min-width: 800px` among **twelve** `max-width` rules. Same result, opposite reading — now widest-first like its neighbours, breaking at 660px where `ReaderLayout` drops its frame.

## After

`screenshot-1788824383097-16.jpg` — 16px padding, no horizontal overflow, single column, value under its label, address intact in both languages.

## Worth saying plainly

`resize_window` reported success three times and never actually changed the viewport — `innerWidth` stayed 1536. My earlier "mobile" screenshots were desktop renders, and I'd have shipped this if you hadn't checked in devtools. I got a true 390px viewport by serving the page inside a sized iframe, which is what produced the real evidence.

1200/1200 tests, 0 type errors, build and brand lint clean, HEAD verified steady either side. Pushed to **#612** (`238e0e7`).

Want me to give Settings the same treatment when I build it — render it at 390px before claiming it's done?

🌱 graft saved ~77k tokens this turn, 1 call.
